1	Cancer dependency research with an autonomous RSI loop
     2	
     3	Goal and executable handoff for a local research agent
     4	
     5	Prepared 28 October 2026. Treat every source below as a seed to verify against the current primary source, release manifest, and paper methods.
     6	
     7	
     8	1 - The ambitious goal
     9	
    10	Build and run a laptop-based autonomous research system that answers a specific, still-open question about when molecularly defined cancer dependencies persist or fail across measured culture environments.
    11	
    12	The primary question is whether measured sensitivity to culture conditions, together with genotype and tumor state, can explain failures of dependency transfer from conventional cancer models to patient-derived organoids beyond lineage and technical variation alone.
    13	
    14	Produce all of the following.
    15	
    16	- At least one previously unreported, precisely bounded, externally supported explanatory finding. It may be a positive conditional dependency rule, a convincing refutation of a meaningful dependency claim, or an informative bound that materially changes how a target should be interpreted. It must resolve a specific uncertainty, not merely increase a benchmark score.
    17	- A reproducible evidence atlas covering every eligible gene in the controlled environmental panel, including support, contradiction, heterogeneity, uncertainty, missing evidence, and excluded genes with reasons. Expansion beyond that selected panel is exploratory unless independently justified.
    18	- A defensible connection between measured environmental sensitivity and transfer behavior in an independently filtered organoid cohort, where the available evidence supports that connection.
    19	- An implemented research-policy improvement loop with real experiments, faithful historical replay, executable policy revisions, fresh deployment, and a final comparison against strong fixed exploration strategies.
    20	- Evidence that the learned policy produces a practically meaningful improvement under matched total resources, including its own learning overhead.
    21	- A manuscript and complete reproducibility package ready for independent expert review, with all findings, failures, limitations, and costs disclosed.
    22	
    23	Seek a finding that changes which cancer target evidence researchers should trust. Do not substitute a generic prediction leaderboard or an agent framework demonstration for that scientific objective.
    24	
    25	Ambition does not authorize changing the standard of evidence. If the scientific result or the policy improvement fails its criteria, the overall goal remains unmet. A valid negative result can qualify only when it resolves a predeclared meaningful uncertainty with sufficient precision. An insignificant p-value does not qualify.
    26	
    27	
    28	2 - Your operating role
    29	
    30	You are the lead investigator, research engineer, statistician, and experiment coordinator for this project.
    31	
    32	Execute the work. Do not stop after writing a plan, creating folders, or describing an architecture. Use the current session to establish the scientific contract, build the smallest working vertical slice, evaluate real public observations, and begin the first actual policy-improvement cycle when the evidence and resources permit.
    33	
    34	Use frontier model reasoning through the capabilities already supplied by your host agent. All scientific fitting, simulation, evaluation, and data processing must run on this laptop. Public web access and public data services are allowed. No new wet-lab measurements, controlled-access patient data, paid scientific cloud compute, or local foundation-model training are required.
    35	
    36	Make routine research and implementation decisions autonomously. Ask only when a missing credential, explicit spending authority, unavailable required file, or genuinely consequential unresolved user choice prevents further authorized work. Complete all independent work first.
    37	
    38	Work inside an isolated project directory named cancer-dependency-rsi under the current workspace, or continue the existing project if its identity is unambiguous. Preserve unrelated files and existing instructions.
    39	
    40	Install dependencies in a project environment. Respect existing permissions and approval controls. Do not copy permission-bypass flags from upstream agent launch scripts. Do not submit papers, publish repositories, contact researchers, purchase services, or provision new infrastructure.
    41	
    42	Use specialist workers when available, with distinct roles for literature and novelty, data provenance, scientific modeling, evaluator implementation, and adversarial review. The evaluator and final data access must have a narrower interface than the proposing agent. Shared privileged access is not a genuine security boundary and must never be described as one.
    43

    46	
    47	Verify and read the methods, data availability, supplements, and closest relevant findings before treating any seed as an established fact.

    85	The starting literature establishes several constraints.
    86	
    87	- The Broad resource reports 147 genome-scale screens, while the Sanger resource reports screens across 162 organoids. These counts are not automatically disjoint biological samples.
    88	- The smaller controlled Broad environmental experiment has 250 deliberately selected test genes and 18 screens across only seven biological models. It includes seven matched format contrasts and five matched medium contrasts, with possible repeated models. Verify the exact design in the source.
    89	- The 250 genes were selected partly because they differed between model environments. They are not a representative genome-wide sample.
    90	- The October 2026 transferability study already examines expression-based transfer from conventional models to Broad and Sanger organoids for 20 selected genes. Generic 2D-to-organoid transfer is not the new contribution.
    91	- Broad's temporary NextGen manuscript dataset was incorporated into DepMap Public 26Q3. Staff direct users to the integrated CRISPRGeneEffect.csv and relevant model metadata. Reverify the current route rather than inventing a file ID or assuming old instructions still work.
    92	- Sanger processed fitness measurements and Broad Chronos gene effects are different measurement systems. Their absolute values are not interchangeable.
    93	- Historical releases, a current integrated release, and independently produced laboratory data are different forms of evidence. Reprocessing the same observations is not biological replication.
    94	
    95	Resolve downloads through current official manifests. Record source URL, release or commit, retrieval date, license, byte size, and checksum. Do not invent direct download URLs or accession metadata. Use official alternative routes if a public portal blocks unattended retrieval. Do not bypass a challenge or access control.
    96	
    97	Build around public processed observations. Raw sequencing is unnecessary. If a proposed analysis requires paired observations that are not actually released, identify that limitation before implementing the model.
    98	
    99	
   100	4 - Hardware, budget, and persistence
   101	
   102	Inspect the available RAM, CPU, disk, operating system, installed runtimes, and already configured model access without printing secrets.
   103	
   104	Set conservative defaults and save them in a machine-readable configuration.
   105	
   106	- No GPU dependency.
   107	- At most two CPU-heavy jobs concurrently.
   108	- An aggregate research memory ceiling of the smaller of 8 GiB and 60 percent of physical RAM, reduced further when necessary to leave the host responsive.
   109	- A ten-minute default timeout for an individual exploratory fitting job. Longer jobs require an explicit recorded allocation from the existing campaign budget.
   110	- A download ceiling of 20 GiB or one quarter of available disk space, whichever is smaller.
   111	- A first pilot target of 24 real evaluated development nodes and three executable policy challengers, retaining the incumbent.
   112	- An eight-hour ceiling for the first pilot invocation. This is a safety ceiling, not a promised completion time.
   113	- No automatic increase in financial, disk, concurrency, or wall-time ceilings.
   114	
   115	Use the host agent's already authorized model access. Any additional programmatic metered API calls require a numeric user-configured cap or an existing explicitly authorized cap. If none exists, the additional API spending cap is zero. Continue with host-driven reasoning and local computation where possible, and build the adapter without dispatching unapproved calls.
   116	
   117	Do not require the user to buy new services just to start the project. Do not silently equate an unknown price with zero.
   118	
   119	For separately dispatched API calls, enforce limits in code. Reserve a conservative maximum cost before each request, count concurrent reservations and retries, reconcile against returned usage, and persist the ledger before dispatch. Do not call a provider whose billable maximum cannot be bounded by the configured limits.
   120	
   121	Record model identifiers, prompts, token counts when exposed, tool costs, wall time, CPU time, and peak memory. If host-model costs cannot be measured, mark them unknown. You may still do science, but you cannot certify an all-in cost improvement while material costs are unobserved.
   122	
   123	Use append-only event records and checkpoint after every completed experiment. Track proposed, dispatched, completed, failed, and committed states. An interrupted request remains reserved until reconciled. Never reset the budget or repeat a completed paid request on resume.
   124	
   125	Do not claim a process is running unless you have an actual live process or job identifier and recent heartbeat. If the host session ends, write the exact next action and resume command. Do not promise work will continue after the runtime stops.
   126	
   127	
   128	5 - Data and identifiability audit
   129	
   130	Before adaptive hypothesis search, construct a provenance table with biological model, donor, tumor lineage, sample origin, laboratory, assay library, medium, growth format, replicate identity, release, and measured outcome.
   131	
   132	Create explicit crosswalks among Broad, HCMI, Sanger, and author-specific identifiers. Mark uncertain donor identity as uncertain rather than assuming independence.
   133	
   134	Determine which observations are truly paired. Count independent biological models and donors. Do not count genes, guide RNAs, wells, alternative cultures, or technical replicates as additional independent patients.
   135	
   136	Audit release composition and preprocessing provenance. An integrated release may contain validation observations or corrections learned jointly from them. Removing overlapping rows alone does not undo leakage through outcome-guided target selection, normalization, or model selection. Prefer compatible study-specific releases and transformations fitted on development data. If a fitted correction used external dependency outcomes, rebuild a development-only analysis or obtain genuinely independent validation evidence. Disclosure alone does not restore independence. Distinguish that outcome leakage from covariate-only joint preprocessing, which must be disclosed as transductive feature preprocessing with appropriately limited claims. This is a required provenance check, not an assertion that any named release is contaminated.
   137	
   138	Verify dependency score direction, dynamic range, controls, missingness, and quality flags separately for each source. Avoid direct subtraction of Chronos values from Sanger fold-change or essentiality scores.
   139	
   140	Preserve the seven-model environmental design as a small, selected experiment. Determine whether row-level paired outcomes, replicates, and required metadata are sufficient for the intended contrast. A batch correction cannot separate laboratory and biology when the experimental design confounds them.
   141	
   142	Record attrition explicitly, including models unable to grow in a condition and genes excluded for insufficient variation or precision.
   143	
   144	Data eligibility is determined from prespecified quality and identifiability rules. It must not be selected later to maximize a favorable result.
   145	
   146	The gate is an identifiable, falsifiable question in a named subset. If the data cannot support the original question, propose and document a narrower still-open question within the same scientific objective. Do not pretend the original broader goal has been achieved.
   147	
   148	
   149	6 - Scientific estimands and research contract
   150	
   151	Start from two connected estimands.
   152	
   153	The direct environmental estimand is the change in a gene's measured dependency between environment A and environment B within the same biological model, while holding the other measured culture condition fixed. Analyze medium and growth format separately where the design permits.
   154	
   155	The transfer estimand is the extent to which a prespecified genotype, tumor-state, or context relationship predicts dependency behavior in an independently filtered organoid cohort beyond lineage and the strongest appropriate baseline.
   156	
   157	Use original documented assay units for paired within-study contrasts. Use justified ranking, calibration, or outcome-specific comparisons for cross-study evidence.
   158	
   159	For each environmental claim, report the dependency in both conditions, all individual paired changes, uncertainty, and heterogeneity. A near-zero average can conceal large opposing effects.
   160	
   161	Do not call a dependency invariant because a difference is nonsignificant. If claiming equivalence, define a scientifically justified equivalence margin before confirmatory evaluation and require the relevant interval to fall inside that margin. If no defensible margin exists, report continuous effects and uncertainty without an invariance label.
   162	
   163	A stable absence of dependency is not a stable cancer vulnerability. Establish that the dependency itself is meaningful in the environments covered by a positive claim.
   164	
   165	Do not interpret a predictive expression feature as a causal mediator without identifying assumptions and suitable evidence. Environmental intervention evidence and cross-cohort biomarker associations must retain distinct evidence labels.
   166	
   167	Carry uncertainty and shared-model dependence in estimated environmental sensitivity into downstream transfer analyses using a justified measurement-error, resampling, or sensitivity analysis. Do not treat noisy estimated sensitivities as exact independent inputs. Report conclusions that change materially across plausible environmental-effect estimates.
   168	
   169	During initial development, choose and justify the precise primary endpoint, practical effect margin, hypothesis family, baseline set, uncertainty procedure, and sensitivity analyses. Then freeze them before policy optimization.
   170	
   171	The research contract must include the following.
   172	
   173	- Exact question and falsifiable alternatives.
   174	- Intended population, environments, targets, and generalization claim.
   175	- Eligibility and exclusion rules.
   176	- Data and identifier versions.
   177	- Development, policy-evaluation, and final external partitions.
   178	- Feature engineering and transformation rules.
   179	- Primary and secondary endpoints with fixed direction.
   180	- Minimum practical effects or equivalence margins and their justification.
   181	- Multiplicity control and uncertainty methods.
   182	- Baseline definitions.
   183	- Invalid-result rules.
   184	- Success, failure, inconclusive, and budget-exhaustion conditions.
   185	
   186	The initial lock fixes the permitted hypothesis and transformation spaces, partitions, evaluator, baseline definitions, practical margins, and inferential rules. Adaptive development may select hypotheses, features, hyperparameters, and fitted artifacts within those spaces. A second lock commits the exact selected claim family, predictions, and artifacts before external evaluation.
   187	
   188	Hash this contract, evaluator code, and split manifests. Changing a locked scientific contract creates a new study identifier and requires appropriate new evaluation evidence.
   189	
   190	
   191	7 - Novelty and biological scope
   192	
   193	Maintain a claim ledger throughout the project.
   194	
   195	For each proposed claim, record the nearest prior result, which part is already established, the precise remaining uncertainty, evidence needed to resolve it, and the consequence if the claim is supported or refuted.
   196	
   197	Read the Broad environmental analyses, the Sanger biomarker analyses, and the October transfer study closely. Their reported lipid, adhesion, state, and dependency findings are controls or prior evidence. Recovering them is not a new discovery.
   198	
   199	Use current primary literature, author data, and official documentation. Date the search and preserve queries and important exclusions. Absence of an exact search hit is not proof that a claim is new.
   200	
   201	Choose a bounded hypothesis family before final evaluation. Consider gene classes with measured environmental sensitivity and adequate overlap, not an unconstrained scan of every feature until a small p-value appears.
   202	
   203	Before finalizing the manuscript, repeat the novelty audit for each surviving exact claim. Preserve contradictions and prior evidence. Do not silently rename a known association to make it appear new.
   204	
   205	The required scientific contribution must be more specific than weak organoid transfer, better average correlation, or successful agent automation.
   206	
   207	
   208	8 - Baselines, inference, and adversarial checks
   209	
   210	Build simple competent baselines before allowing elaborate models.
   211	
   212	Before the final lock, reproduce baselines only on development data or independent control data. Any reproduction requiring final external outcomes must occur after the final hypotheses, predictions, artifacts, and inferential code are committed, alongside the final evaluation. Those results cannot inform revisions to the tested study.
   213	
   214	Where applicable compare lineage only, genotype only, tumor-state or expression only, genotype plus state, measured context or assay covariates, and a regularized linear predictor modeled on the existing transfer study.
   215	
   216	Use the same eligible observations and permitted information for each comparison. Learn preprocessing, feature selection, dimension reduction, and tuning within development folds. Do not optimize a feature representation on final external outcomes.
   217	
   218	Compare against the strongest applicable baseline, not only the weakest. If environmental information is central to the explanation, include a prespecified ablation removing it.
   219	
   220	Use effect sizes and calibrated predictive or uncertainty endpoints as the scientific evaluator's optimization target. Do not reward p-value reduction, the number of discoveries, manuscript length, or confidence of the LLM explanation.
   221	
   222	Treat adaptive development as exploratory. Evaluate a locked final claim family once on independent outcomes. For a small confirmatory family, Holm correction at familywise alpha 0.05 is a reasonable default. Any alternative must be justified and frozen before outcomes are revealed.
   223	
   224	Do not apply ordinary fixed-family correction to an indefinitely adaptive stream of repeatedly inspected p-values and call it confirmatory evidence.
   225	
   226	Use uncertainty at the donor or biological-model level, accounting for repeated cultures and target or pathway dependence where relevant. Many bootstrap repetitions do not create new biological replication. With few clusters, assess whether the proposed interval or test is justified and report the effective sample size.
   227	
   228	Perform relevant negative controls, leakage checks, donor and lineage sensitivity analyses, platform sensitivity, and leave-one-model-out checks. Permutations must respect exchangeability and grouping. Do not permute labels freely when the design makes that invalid.
   229	
   230	Synthetic data may test code, calibration, and identifiability under explicit assumptions. Synthetic labels, imputed outcomes, and LLM guesses cannot serve as independent biological validation.
   231	
   232	Only make claims supported by the actual evidence. Public dependency screens alone do not establish clinical efficacy, normal-tissue safety, treatment resistance reversal, or universal target validity.
   233	
   234	
   235	9 - Three distinct evaluation layers
   236	
   237	Keep these layers separate.
   238	
   239	A - Development task panels
   240	
   241	Use them to build scientific artifacts, tune development models, generate discovery trees, and select policy challengers. Record every adaptive use.
   242	
   243	B - Reserved policy evaluation panels
   244	
   245	Use them to compare the final learned exploration policy with fixed strategies in fresh rollouts. Freeze the compared policies and selection criterion before these panels are evaluated.
   246	
   247	C - Final external biological evaluation
   248	
   249	Prefer an independently filtered Sanger cohort after resolving donor overlap, release provenance, assay compatibility, and adequate representation. Use final outcomes only after committing the hypotheses, predictions, model artifacts, and inferential code.
   250	
   251	A final external cohort cannot also be a repeatedly consulted policy reward. Do not send final Sanger outcomes into the replay pool.
   252	
   253	For each final claim, identify exactly which component each dataset validates. External confirmation of dependency transfer does not independently validate a medium or format effect, or establish that environmental sensitivity caused transfer failure. Retain adaptively reused environmental evidence as exploratory or selection-adjusted evidence, as justified. Do not manufacture an independent environmental test by splitting genes from the same seven models. Seek an additional existing public controlled-environment dataset when the selected claim requires independent environmental confirmation. If none is suitable, narrow the claim or retain the unmet evidence gate.
   254	
   255	Subdividing the selected 250 genes does not create hundreds of independent biological tasks. Record model, donor, gene, and pathway overlap in all panels, and use blocked evaluation. The larger development cohorts may provide engineering tasks for policy learning, but their transfer to the small environmental problem must be reported honestly.
   256	
   257	Within a single privileged local agent, enforce a logged protocol with a separate evaluator interface and restricted inputs. Do not claim cryptographic secrecy or genuine blindness merely because an outcome file lives in a separate directory.
   258	
   259	Use retrospective external validation as the default wording. Public literature and model pretraining can expose outcomes. Record known exposure and do not certify that public results were unknowable.
   260	
   261	A failed final test is a failed final test. Subsequent work that uses its outcomes becomes exploratory unless genuinely new independent evidence is obtained.
   262	
   263	
   264	10 - Implement the actual RSI loop
   265	
   266	Keep the base scientific generator, its model version and prompting contract, data contract, and evaluator fixed during a policy comparison.
   267	
   268	Make the editable policy an executable module that receives observed history, legal actions, and remaining resources, and selects an action.
   269	
   270	Legal actions may include opening a predefined analysis family, choosing an existing branch, refining a particular artifact, running a permitted diagnostic, and stopping.
   271	
   272	The policy may alter branching, prioritization, exploration versus refinement, and stopping. It cannot change labels, splits, metrics, practical margins, multiplicity correction, or success criteria.
   273	
   274	A narrative reflection is not a policy improvement unless it changes executed decisions.
   275	
   276	Record each discovery node's immutable parent, exact artifact, input context hash, data and split hashes, evaluator hash, seeds, result, validity diagnostics, failures, model calls, and measured costs.
   277	
   278	Historical replay may reveal only previously executed artifacts and their actual recorded outcomes. It must not use a model to invent outcomes for unexplored analyses.
   279	
   280	A reordered branch may alter the context seen by a generator. Make refinement depend on an immutable parent and fixed context, or require an exact context match before replaying a recorded child. Do not assume a recorded child represents an arbitrary counterfactual generation.
   281	
   282	The replay policy sees only the outcomes revealed along its trajectory. Do not expose the full tree's future rewards.
   283	
   284	Mark unsupported replay actions unsupported. Do not assign them fake scores or treat a surrogate prediction as a measured outcome. Compare policies on common support, report support coverage, and use replay as a screening tool.
   285	
   286	Perform the following cycle.
   287	
   288	1. Run the initial fixed policy on real development tasks.
   289	2. Preserve the evaluated discovery trees as replay worlds.
   290	3. Generate at least three executable policy challengers plus the unchanged incumbent.
   291	4. Replay them under the same resource constraints and support rules.
   292	5. Select a challenger with the frozen selection rule.
   293	6. Test the challenger in fresh development rollouts against fixed exploration using the same generator and evaluator.
   294	7. Promote only when the preregistered criterion is met.
   295	8. Retain the incumbent when challengers fail.
   296	9. Add only development histories and repeat.
   297	
   298	Complete at least two genuine cycles before the final policy comparison if the authorized resources and valid tasks permit. Two cycles do not require two promotions. An unchanged incumbent is a valid experimental outcome.
   299	
   300	After development, freeze the best admissible policy and evaluate it on the reserved policy panels. Compare it with the original fixed exploration strategy and at least one simple fixed-allocation or random-selection strategy.
   301	
   302	
   303	11 - What counts as demonstrated policy improvement
   304	
   305	Predeclare one primary operating point or cost-to-quality endpoint. Also report complete scientific-quality-versus-cost curves.
   306	
   307	Use the same generator, evaluator, initial artifacts, information permissions, and common resource ceilings for all policies.
   308	
   309	Charge policy rewriting, replay, failed jobs, promotion trials, and extra model calls to the improving system. Permit fixed baselines to spend the corresponding budget on scientific search.
   310	
   311	Report both end-to-end performance including learning overhead and deployment-only performance with learning costs shown separately.
   312	
   313	The ambitious engineering target is at least 20 percent lower total measured API expenditure to reach a predeclared valid scientific-quality threshold, under the same CPU ceiling and information constraints, compared with the strongest fixed baseline. This is a project target, not a forecast.
   314	
   315	Set the quality threshold from development evidence before final policy evaluation. It must be meaningful and attainable by competent baselines, not chosen after observing which policy wins.
   316	
   317	Use paired blocked comparisons where appropriate and report uncertainty. For the default 20 percent savings goal, require the prespecified one-sided 95 percent lower confidence bound on savings to meet the 20 percent practical margin. A point estimate above 20 percent with a lower bound merely above zero supports some improvement but does not meet that ambitious margin. Freeze how failures to reach the quality threshold within budget are treated as censored outcomes. Do not convert nonattainment into invented exact costs. Random seeds quantify execution variability, not independent biological replication.
   318	
   319	If API expenditure is not the dominant or measurable resource, choose a justified alternative primary resource endpoint during the initial contract stage, explain it, and lock it before optimization. All other material resources must still be measured or strictly matched. A CPU-only advantage or token proxy cannot satisfy C9 while material host-model costs remain unknown and unmatched. In that case retain an unresolved cost gate and avoid claiming all-in savings. Define an equally explicit practical improvement margin and uncertainty requirement for any alternative endpoint. Do not switch endpoints after seeing final results.
   320	
   321	If faithful replay has inadequate support, preserve that finding and use fresh rollouts to assess the proposed policy. Label the method accurately as a Dream-RSI-inspired adaptation and disclose departures.
   322	
   323	Do not call the system recursively self-improving merely because more compute improved a reused validation score.
   324	
   325	
   326	12 - Completion criteria
   327	
   328	Mark the ambitious goal complete only when every applicable criterion below has documentary evidence.
   329	
   330	C1 - A current novelty audit identifies a precise unresolved cancer dependency question and distinguishes it from the August resources and October transfer study.
   331	
   332	C2 - All analyses use legitimately accessible public data, with complete provenance, licensing, identifier crosswalks, and reproducible retrieval or documented local cache installation.
   333	
   334	C3 - The intended paired contrast or conditional relationship is identifiable within a named population. Confounding and selection are disclosed, and independent biological units are counted correctly.
   335	
   336	C4 - The scientific contract, eligibility rules, splits, baseline set, practical effects, evaluator, and confirmatory procedures were frozen before adaptive optimization and final evaluation.
   337	
   338	C5 - The pipeline reproduces relevant published or author-code baseline results closely enough to establish outcome direction, cohort integrity, and measurement interpretation, with discrepancies resolved or explicitly bounded.
   339	
   340	C6 - At least one previously unreported explanatory finding passes the frozen scientific criteria and relevant external tests. A supported refutation or informative bound may qualify when it resolves a meaningful predeclared uncertainty. Mere nonsignificance, a rediscovered association, or a better exploratory score does not qualify.
   341	
   342	C7 - The evidence atlas covers all eligible genes in the controlled panel and lists every exclusion. Every entry distinguishes dependency strength, environmental change, uncertainty, heterogeneity, biomarker evidence, transfer evidence, and prior knowledge.
   343	
   344	C8 - At least two real policy-improvement cycles have run, with executable challengers, faithful replay, fresh rollout evaluation, retained failed attempts, and a final frozen-policy comparison on reserved panels.
   345	
   346	C9 - The learned policy meets the preregistered practical improvement criterion against the strongest fixed baseline under matched total resources. Meeting only a deployment-only criterion does not satisfy an end-to-end claim.
   347	
   348	C10 - Scientific conclusions survive the prespecified multiplicity correction, appropriate uncertainty analysis, key ablations, and adversarial checks. Any claim of invariance requires positive dependency evidence and justified equivalence evidence.
   349	
   350	C11 - A clean reproduction run regenerates the primary estimates, figures, evidence decisions, and policy comparison within documented tolerances from frozen artifacts. It must not require rerunning stochastic LLM search to reproduce the reported analysis.
   351

SECTION Sec6 Culture conditions and screen outcomesTo better understand the combined dataset of NextGen and traditional models, we studied differences in gene essentiality between NextGen 3D organoids and traditional 2D models. We compared 3D organoids grown in Matrigel domes with serum-free media (containing EGF and FGF10) to lineage-matched 2D adherent models cultured directly on plastic with serum-containing media (referred to as 3D (n = 94) and 2D (n = 433) models, respectively). We maintained consistent culture conditions in each cohort to elucidate the effects of these conditions.Examination of dependencies on frequently mutated oncogenes and TSGs (mutated in >1% in TCGA53) revealed increased CDK4 dependency in 2D models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.26, mean 2D dependency score = –0.83, q = 9.54 × 10−21; Extended Data Fig. 8d,e), which probably reflects greater reliance on this cell cycle driver in these fast-growing models. Similarly, MDM2 dependency was enriched in 2D models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.27, mean 2D dependency score = –0.54, q = 4.23 × 10−12; Extended Data Fig. 8d,e), which held for TP53 wild-type (WT) models (mean 3D dependency score = –0.54, mean 2D dependency score = –1.09, P = 8.26 × 10−4). This result suggests that 2D culture conditions trigger p53 activation, an effect exposed by reduced MDM2-mediated p53 degradation.Summarizing pathway-level differences in gene dependencies53 revealed that most 2D models (65.6%) showed positive mean dependency scores for p53 pathway TSGs (TP53 and ATM) compared with only 21.3% of 3D models (Extended Data Fig. 8f,g). This result further suggests that the p53 pathway is more growth-suppressive in 2D than 3D culture conditions. Conversely, knockout of a TSG did not generally cause a stronger growth benefit in 3D organoids than in 2D models, a result that is in contrast to a previous study analysing serum-containing spheroid cultures22 (Extended Data Fig. 8d,f).To broadly compare gene essentialities, we calculated the difference in mean dependency scores between 3D and 2D models for every gene (n = 16,691; excluding common essential genes), and identified gene sets (Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB; q < 0.05) that were significantly overrepresented at the extremes of this difference (Fig. 5a,b). Clustering these gene sets by component overlap (>0.3; Extended Data Fig. 8h) merged two sets (adhesion and cytoskeleton (adhesion–cytoskeleton), and cell cycle), whereas five others (lipid metabolism, mTORC1, oxidative phosphorylation, UV response and systemic lupus erythematosus) remained separate.Fig. 5Comparing 2D and 3D dependencies to disentangle the effects of culture conditions.a,b, Gene sets enriched for differential dependencies between 3D and 2D models (n = 94 (3D) and 433 (2D)). Odds ratios for the 9 significant gene sets (q < 0.05) overrepresented in the 200 outlier genes were plotted, clustered and coloured by gene overlap (>0.3; a). Mean dependency differences and their significance for individual genes (two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test; gene n = 3,521), coloured by the gene set clusters from a were also plotted (b). c–e, Minipool screens were performed to elucidate the differing effects of growth format and culture medium. A minipool screen (250 test genes) was designed (c) to separate the effects of growth format (plastic versus dome) and culture medium (RPMI–FBS versus OPAC) on gene essentiality. The screens identified genes for which dependencies are primarily altered by growth format (d) or culture medium (e), with red dashed lines indicating significance threshold (q = 0.05, two-sided linear regression t-test) and the point colours indicating gene classes in the minipool library (bottom). Screen n = 11 (dome), 7 (plastic), 9 (OPAC), 9 (RPMI–FBS). f,g, Comparisons across growth formats and culture media. f, Different gene classes represented in the minipool library are highlighted. Integrin and actin regulation classes exhibited significant variance across growth formats. g, By contrast, lipid metabolism class were affected by culture medium (q < 0.05, two-tailed F-test; gene n = 200). h, Differential effects on integrin and cholesterol homeostasis dependencies assessed by viability after test gene knockout. Values are the mean ± s.d. (n = 3). P values calculated using two-tailed two-way ANOVA. R–F, RPMI–FBS. i, Colocalization of integrin chains (green) with FAK (red) in KP3 cells under plastic or dome growth conditions (both in RPMI–FBS). Nuclei (blue) and actin (white) are also shown. Representative images from three independent experiments are displayed. Scale bar, 20 μm.Source dataWe focused on the adhesion–cytoskeleton and lipid metabolism gene sets owing to their probable connection to the physical and metabolic culture environments, respectively. The 3D versus 2D growth format difference plausibly affects cell–cell and cell–extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions and associated dependencies54. By contrast, differential lipid content in media—2D models use lipid-rich RPMI supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), whereas organoid media contain only linoleic and linolenic acids and lack cholesterol—probably influences lipid-metabolism dependencies.Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 9a and Supplementary Table 3). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig. 9b).After applying Chronos to the minipool screen data (which correlated well with genome-wide data, r > 0.59; Extended Data Fig. 9c), we used linear regression to distinguish growth-format and culture-medium effects. This analysis identified seven genes for which dependencies were altered by growth formats (q < 0.05), including three integrin subunits (ITGB1, ITGAV and ITGA3) and two actin regulators (NCKAP1 and PTK2; Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 9d). Eight genes also exhibited dependency changes across different media, three of which regulate lipid metabolism (SPTLC1, SPTLC2 and SQLE; Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 9e).A global analysis of the minipool screen results across the nine functional gene classes did not reveal collective enhancement or impairment of dependencies between different growth formats and media, except for a minor enhancement (Δdependency = 0.09) in the actin regulation class under RPMI–FBS conditions compared with OPAC (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g). To capture opposing effects in gene classes (for example, ITGB1 dependency increases whereas ITGAV decreases in dome culture), we analysed the variance in dependency score differences between conditions (dome versus plastic and OPAC versus RPMI–FBS). Growth format had significantly larger effects on integrin (q = 7.3 × 10−5) and actin regulation genes (q = 7.2 × 10−14), whereas culture medium significantly affected lipid metabolism genes (q = 1.5 × 10−4; Fig. 5f,g). These data demonstrate functional class-specific effects of growth format and medium.To validate these findings, we knocked out ITB1, ITGAV, MSMO1 or SQLE in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies (MSMO1 and SQLE) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies (ITGAV and ITGB1) were sensitive to growth format (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by ITGB1) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by ITGAV) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats55.Notably, neither growth format nor medium significantly affected dependencies on the WNT signalling regulators FZD5 and WLS (Fig. 5f), which were essential only in organoids with high PDAC-classical/MUC program levels (Fig. 4f,g). This result probably reflects stable maintenance of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in organoids rather than its rapid induction by the short-term shift in culture conditions. This result is in contrast to integrin, actin and lipid metabolism dependencies, which seem to be more responsive to acute changes in growth conditions. Together, these findings highlight how dependencies on specific cellular processes vary with culture environment and underscore the importance of selecting appropriate model systems for the biological question being pursued.
SECTION Sec9 Source and culture conditions of NextGen cancer modelsThe source of each of the NextGen models is provided in Supplementary Table 1. In brief, breast cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratories of A.V.L., S.O. and D.L.S. Most of the NextGen CNS tumour models were derived by the laboratory of K.L.L. Colorectal and oesophagus–stomach cancer organoid models were derived by staff at the Cancer Cell Line Factory at the Broad Institute. Ovarian and uterus cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratory of S.J.H. Pancreas cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratories of A.J.A. and S.R. Prostate cancer organoid models were derived by the laboratory of H.B. and the laboratory of Y. Chen. Additional models derived by the HCMI were obtained via the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Models were confirmed for the absence of mycoplasma contamination (Mycoplasma PCR Detection kit; ABM, G238) and authenticated by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling (LabCorp) before expansion. These procedures were repeated monthly during expansion and screening.Organoid media were prepared using the recommendations provided for each of the models (Supplementary Table 1). The conditioned media were prepared by culturing WNT3A-producing L cells (L Wnt-3A; ATCC, CRL-2647) and R-spondin-1-producing 293T cells (Cultrex R-spondin 1 (RSPO1) cells; Trevigen, 3710-001-K) in DMEM with 10% serum. After reaching 80% confluency, cells were washed once with PBS and incubated with Advanced DMEM–F12 medium (Thermo Fisher, 12634028) containing 100 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 1% 100× Glutamax (Ad+++) for another week. The conditioned medium from this culture was then collected, filtered and stored at –80 °C before being used for organoid cultures. All organoids were grown initially as domes composed of 75% growth-factor-reduced, Phenol Red-free Matrigel (50 μl per dome; Corning, 356231) in the recommended medium diluted 1:1 with Ad+++. The screening of organoids was conducted either in Matrigel dome cultures or in adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates (see the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’ below).The NextGen CNS models were grown in tumour stem medium, the composition of which is described in Supplementary Table 1. The conditioned medium was collected routinely during expansion and preserved for subsequent cultures. Cells were seeded in a mixture of 30% conditioned medium and 70% fresh medium. Some of the models were tested for their ability to grow on a Matrigel-coated plate. In brief, cells were plated in 1% Matrigel-coated flasks and cells attached to the coating were carried forward as adherent models. Models that failed to attach to coated plates were grown as spheroids in ultra-low attachment (ULA) vessels (Corning, 3814). Models that were initially derived as adherent cultures on laminin-coated plates were maintained in the same conditions. To coat plates, Matrigel or laminin (Corning, 354232) was diluted in ice-cold PBS at a concentration of 1%. This solution was then added to culture vessels at approximately one-half the recommended volume of medium for a given vessel (for example, 5 ml solution in a T75 flask). Flasks were incubated at 37 °C overnight, and the solution was aspirated immediately before plating the cells. The growth format of each model is listed in Supplementary Table 1.
SECTION Sec21 Comparison of gene expression profiles between spheroid and adherent cultures of the NextGen CNS modelsNine NextGen CNS models were adapted to grow as adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates (coat culture) for 4 weeks or more. RNA samples were collected both before and after adaptation and profiled by RNA-seq using a similar protocol as described above. For these 18 samples (nine models × two conditions (spheroid and coat)), a correlation matrix was calculated based on the expression of the top 10% highly variable genes (n = 1,919). Subsequently, hierarchical clustering of the correlation matrix was conducted using the hclust and heatmap.2 functions in R (Extended Data Fig. 4c). To compare the expression levels of individual genes between the nine samples of spheroid culture and the nine samples of coat culture, the difference in expression levels of all the genes measured in this analysis (n = 19,193) were analysed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (Extended Data Fig. 4f).
SECTION Sec33 Lentiviral production for the minipool screen and its validationLentiviral production was conducted using 293FT cells (Thermo Fisher, R70007) in accordance with the ‘Lentiviral Production in Flasks’ protocol available at the Broad Institute GPP web portal (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols). In brief, the lentiviral particles were generated by the co-transfecting the lentiviral plasmid with a packaging plasmid (psPAX2; 12260, Addgene) and VSV-G envelope (pMD2.G; Addgene, 12259) into 293FT cells using PEIpro transfection reagent (Polyplus, 101000033). The medium was replaced 12 h after transfection, and the virus-containing medium was collected after 36–48 h.
SECTION Sec34 Library preparation for minipool screensFor the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig. 5a,b). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome, https://adhesome.org/); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig. 9a. We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table 3). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.
SECTION Sec35 Minipool screeningBefore screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (<2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time <120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.For the screen, selected models were infected with the amount of library virus required for infecting 30% of the cells in accordance with the result of virus titration on day 0. The infected cells were selected with the concentration of puromycin determined in the puromycin titration between day 1 and day 4. On day 4, cells were seeded into up to 4 conditions (2D monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS (RPMI–FBS); plastic culture with 1:1 OPAC; 3D Matrigel dome culture (dome culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS; and dome culture with 1:1 OPAC), depending on how many conditions survived the above-mentioned selection criteria for the respective model. For plastic culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 10 ml of the respective medium and seeded on a Falcon 100 mm TC-treated cell culture dish (Corning, 53003). For dome culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 0.5 m of the medium used for the condition and subsequently mixed with 1.5 ml of Matrigel. Approximately 40 domes, each with 50 µl of Matrigel–cell suspension were placed on a 100 mm TC-treated culture dish, which was followed by the incubation of the plate at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. Subsequently, 10 ml of the culture medium was added before further incubation. We prepared two technical replicates per each condition.These cultures were maintained until day 14 with refreshment of the medium every 3 days. If the culture showed signs of confluency (coverage of more than 80% of the bottom surface by the cells for monolayer culture on plastic plates and appearance of a dark spot in the middle of the domes for Matrigel dome culture), we passaged the cells instead of replacing the medium while keeping the number of cells after passaging to 2 million cells per dish. Trypsinization (with 0.25% trypsin and 0.1% EDTA (Corning, 25-053-CI)) was used for the passaging of cells in plastic cultures, whereas cells in dome cultures were passaged in accordance with the strategy described above in the section ‘Source and culture conditions of NextGen cancer models’. At day 14, cells were collected by trypsinization and counted. gDNA samples were prepared from these cells and the abundance of individual sgRNA sequences in the genome of these cells were analysed by PCR amplification of the sgRNA sequences, preparation of sequencing libraries from the PCR products and subsequent sequencing of these libraries as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening for gDNA isolation and sequencing’.
SECTION Sec36 Minipool screen analysisMinipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described23, with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. Subsequently, we modelled the Chronos score Yg,k for each gene g and screen k with the generalized linear regression model:\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${Y}_{g,k}={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{d}{I}_{d}+{\beta }_{s}{I}_{s}+{\beta }_{{ds}}{I}_{d}{I}_{s}+\sum _{m\in M}{\beta }_{m}{I}_{m}$$\end{document}Yg,k=β0+βdId+βsIs+βdsIdIs+∑m∈MβmImThe first term captures the baseline viability effect of knocking out gene g. The second and third terms capture the growth format effect and medium effect, where Id and Is are indicator variables representing the types of growth format (Matrigel dome culture (dome) versus monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic)) and culture medium (serum-free OPAC medium versus serum-containing RPMI–FBS medium), respectively. The fourth term captures interaction effects between these two conditions, and the final term captures model effects to account for multiple screens in the same cell line. Differences in effect sizes across growth format and serum status were extracted as βd and βs, respectively. Significance values corresponding to the same coefficients were extracted from the P values calculated using two-sided linear regression t-test.To assess the effects of growth format (or culture medium) on the core functional classes of gene targets included in our minipool library, we calculated the variance in βd (or βs) across members of the same class and compared it to the variance in βd (or βs) across all non-control genes outside of class. For each gene set, we tested whether the in-class variance was significantly greater than the out-of-class variance using one-tailed F-tests.

SECTION Sec16 Organoid cultureOrganoids were maintained either in 80% BME-2 droplets or in 5% BME-2 suspension culture38. In the 80% BME-2 culture, organoids were cultured as described above. For the 5% suspension method, cancer organoids were suspended in a medium/extracellular matrix (ECM) dilution. For example, combining 10 ml of medium with 500 μl of BME-2 achieved the desired concentration, and organoids were then cultured in ultra-low-adherent flasks or plates.For passaging, the medium, cells and ECM were collected and centrifuged at 800g for 2 min. After discarding the supernatant, organoids were dissociated using TrypLE (Gibco 12604013), an enzymatic reagent. The suspension was incubated for 10–60 min, allowing dissociation into small clumps. The cells were then pelleted and replated as described64.

SECTION sec2dot10-biology-15-01782 2.10. Statistical AnalysisStatistical analyses preserved the prespecified role and strongest available biological independence unit of each study layer. In the development, locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, and Sanger-148 analyses, the primary rank-based measure was the Spearman correlation between predicted and observed outcomes for each target and the arithmetic mean of the 20 target correlations (macro target-wise Spearman correlation). MAE, RMSE, R2, calibration intercept, and calibration slope were secondary diagnostics in the development, locked-holdout, and Broad analyses and did not reopen model selection. Because Sanger-corrected LFC and DepMap/Broad Chronos Gene Effect values were not treated as numerically equivalent, the Sanger validation and cross-cohort synthesis were based on rank correlation rather than absolute-scale error. Target-wise correlation operates across organoids for each gene; within-organoid correlation instead operates across the 20 genes for each organoid. Averaging target-wise correlations does not test within-organoid gene ranking. The original analysis hierarchy, inferential units, resampling procedures, and multiplicity rules are summarized in Table S9; the retrospective within-organoid endpoints are defined in Section 2.10.1 and Tables S17–S19.Resampling units followed the available biological grouping. Development and locked 2D holdout uncertainty used 2000 PatientID-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all models from a sampled patient group together. Broad-94 used 5000 model-level bootstrap replicates within OncotreeLineage strata because PatientID was unavailable in the original evaluation records; the later partial-donor sensitivities are reported separately in Section 2.10.3. Sanger-148 used 5000 donor-cluster bootstrap replicates, retaining all organoids from a sampled donor together. Tiriac tumor-normal comparisons used 5000 case-level bootstrap replicates within the 38-tumor and 11-normal groups. Unless otherwise specified, 95% percentile CIs were defined by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Paired model comparisons used common resampling indices. The standard error used in the development one-standard-error rule was derived from the 2000-replicate PatientID-cluster bootstrap distribution of OOF predictions.For permutation analyses, predictions remained fixed and complete 20-target observed-outcome vectors were moved without disrupting the prespecified biological grouping. The locked 2D sensitivity analysis used 2000 one-sided permutations of patient-aggregated outcome vectors within OncotreeLineage strata. Broad-94 used 5000 one-sided permutations of ModelID-level outcome vectors within lineage. Sanger-148 used 5000 two-sided permutations after donor averaging, with donor-level outcome vectors moved within tumor-type/lineage strata and the absolute macro correlation used as the test statistic. Empirical p-values used the standard plus-one numerator and denominator correction. Broad and Sanger target-specific permutation p-values were adjusted separately within their 20-target families using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure.In the retrospective cross-cohort synthesis, common-positive direction was assessed with a one-sided exact binomial benchmark (n = 20; null probability = 0.50), interpreted descriptively because targets were correlated and the synthesis was retrospective. Target-specific correlations were pooled on the Fisher-z scale using inverse-variance fixed-effect weights derived from cohort-specific bootstrap uncertainty, and the 20 two-sided meta-analytic p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Random-effects estimates and I2 were descriptive because only two cohorts were available. Target-panel sensitivity used 20,000 target-bootstrap resamples, while cross-target dependence was assessed using 50,000 one-sided simultaneous block permutations at the Broad ModelID and Sanger donor-mean levels. Expression-only-minus-lineage target differences were evaluated separately in Broad and Sanger using one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. None of these retrospective analyses was interpreted as a new validation cohort.In the Tiriac layer, two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests compared patient-level tumor and normal projections for each target. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR adjustment was applied across 20 tests. Cliff’s delta described effect direction. Concordance between the Tiriac tumor target-median vector and the Broad and Sanger target-median prediction vectors was evaluated using two-sided Spearman correlations across 20 targets. We used PCA and SMD measures only as descriptive domain-shift diagnostics, and they did not inform the confirmatory decision.A retrospective coverage-threshold sensitivity analysis compared the prespecified 80% rule with stricter 90% and 95% requirements using the archived target-specific present-feature counts. The number of eligible models among the fixed 20 targets was recorded for each external cohort. Only the eligibility requirement was varied; no features were removed, no models were refitted, and no missing-feature handling was changed (Table S16).Tests were two-sided unless explicitly prespecified as one-sided. Within each stated 20-target family, FDR q < 0.05 defined the multiplicity-adjusted target-level significance; exact p-values, effect sizes, and CIs were reported together where applicable. Exploratory and post hoc analyses retained those labels even when a statistical threshold was crossed, and no analysis result changed the target panel, feature identities, hyperparameters, primary metrics, or previously generated predictions. Analyses were implemented in Python 3.12.13 using NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.2.3, SciPy 1.17.0, scikit-learn 1.8.0, and joblib 1.5.3. Random seeds, environment files, protocols, SHA-256 manifests, and integrity checks were preserved in the archived reproducibility package.2.10.1. Retrospective Evaluation of Gene Ranking Within OrganoidsA retrospective secondary analysis evaluated whether the frozen expression-only predictions ranked the 20 genes within individual organoids in agreement with measured CRISPR outcomes. This secondary analysis was defined after the external outcomes were available and was not a new blinded validation. It retained all 20 targets and all 94 Broad and 148 Sanger organoids; Tiriac was excluded because measured dependency outcomes were unavailable. No predictions, models, features, hyperparameters, or targets were changed, and the original target-wise primary analysis was retained.For each organoid, we calculated Spearman correlation across its 20 predicted and 20 observed scores, using average ranks for ties, and summarized the correlations by their arithmetic mean. Lower scores denoted stronger measured or predicted dependency. The main comparator assigned every organoid the same per-gene mean of the observed outcomes across all 852 2D training models, with each training model weighted equally. This fixed ranking tested whether expression predictions improved on gene-level average dependency. We also reused the archived lineage-only predictions: the ridge reference in Broad and patient-weighted 2D lineage means in Sanger. No external outcomes were used to fit either comparator (Table S17).To examine a short candidate list, we calculated the overlap between the three lowest predicted scores and the three lowest measured scores, divided by three, within each organoid. The cohort mean was expressed as a percentage. Ties at the selection boundary were to be resolved by the fixed target identifiers; none occurred. Expression-minus-comparator differences were calculated within the same organoids for both the full-ranking correlation and top-three overlap (Table S18). These endpoints assess agreement with measured CRISPR score ordering within the selected panel, not cancer selectivity, cross-gene calibration, drug response, or clinical benefit.We estimated 95% percentile CIs using 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples: organoid models sampled within observed lineage strata for Broad, and donor clusters sampled with all their organoids retained together for Sanger. The Sanger main estimate remained organoid-weighted. A donor-level sensitivity analysis first averaged the predicted and observed 20-gene vectors within each of 144 donors, then recalculated both endpoints with equal donor weights and a 10,000-replicate donor bootstrap (Table S19). Seeds were 20260928, 20260929, and 20260930 for Broad, Sanger, and donor-mean sensitivity, respectively. All correlations were defined. Intervals were conditional on the frozen models and fixed panel; they did not include model-training or gene-panel selection uncertainty. The secondary comparisons were not adjusted for multiplicity and were interpreted as exploratory.2.10.2. Retrospective Sensitivity to Missing-Feature Imputation in TiriacA retrospective sensitivity analysis evaluated the effects of alternative missing-feature replacement values on Tiriac projections. This descriptive analysis was not prespecified. The archived code represented absent inputs as NaN and applied the frozen training-median imputer, followed by the stored scaler and Elastic Net estimator. This pipeline reproduced all 1100 archived Tiriac predictions exactly. The reference predictions were generated with training medians and were retained for comparison with the alternative imputation methods. The 39 absent unique features corresponded to 0–8 missing predictors per target, with the same missing-feature pattern across all 55 samples.Using the same frozen models, we compared training-median imputation with two alternatives: zero on the log2(TPM + 1) scale before standardization, and the stored training-reference mean for each feature. These means were estimated after median imputation in the 852-model training data and correspond to zero standardized input, up to floating-point rounding. Only absent features were replaced; observed expression values, including measured zeros, were retained. We summarized absolute projection changes, Spearman correlation across the 20 genes within each profile, and top-three set overlap relative to the median-imputed reference. We evaluated sample-level results and case-averaged profiles, including 38 tumor and 11 normal cases. We also repeated the original tumor–normal comparisons using the same 5000 bootstrap resamples (seed 20260830), Mann–Whitney tests, and 20-target FDR adjustment. These are descriptive checks of projection stability, not prediction accuracy. Because the models are linear and the missing-feature pattern is shared, constant replacement values create a common offset per target; preservation of within-target sample ranks and tumor–normal differences is therefore expected algebraically (Tables S20 and S21).2.10.3. Retrospective Broad Donor Audit and Sensitivity AnalysesA retrospective metadata audit linked 16 of the 94 models to 15 PatientID values in the supplied DepMap Model.csv and nine additional models to nine source-specific donor identifiers in the archived Sanger exclusion registry. Thus, donor information was available for 25 models, forming 24 source-specific groups, while 69 models remained unresolved. ACH-002883 and ACH-002884 shared PatientID PT-N65Hvq. The DepMap and Sanger donor namespaces could not be fully reconciled, so the 24 groups do not establish 24 independently verified biological donors. No donor identity was inferred from lineage or model-name similarity (Table S22).Retrospective sensitivity analyses used the unchanged predictions, outcomes, and 20-gene panel. Each member of the known same-donor pair was omitted in turn. A conditional full-cohort bootstrap grouped the known pair and treated unresolved models as singleton units, yielding 93 resampling groups; this assumption does not establish independence of the 69 unresolved models. In the donor-documented subset, model-level and donor-cluster bootstraps were compared on the same 25 models, and a separate analysis averaged prediction, outcome, and lineage-reference vectors within the 24 source-specific donor groups before evaluation. All analyses used 5000 paired bootstrap replicates within the observed OncotreeLineage strata (seed 20260929), retaining every model from each sampled group. Percentile 95% intervals were calculated at 2.5% and 97.5%. Target-wise correlations were reranked within each resample and averaged across all 20 targets; an undefined target correlation contributed zero, following the archived convention. Organoid weighting was retained except in the donor-mean analysis. Full-cohort and known-subset model-level replays with the same seed provide matched references; they do not replace the original CIs. Tables S23 and S24 report the primary target-wise and secondary within-organoid endpoints. These post hoc intervals were not adjusted for multiple sensitivity comparisons, and no new confirmatory permutation or FDR claim was made.

SECTION sec3dot7-biology-15-01782 3.7. Retrospective Gene Ranking Within Individual OrganoidsUsing the unchanged 20-gene predictions, the mean within-organoid Spearman correlation was 0.3428 (95% CI, 0.3026 to 0.3826) in Broad-94 and 0.4294 (95% CI, 0.3926 to 0.4645) in Sanger-148 (Table S17). The corresponding fixed 2D-mean comparator estimates were 0.2057 and 0.1995. Paired expression-minus-fixed-mean differences were +0.1371 (95% CI, 0.0987 to 0.1780) and +0.2299 (95% CI, 0.1981 to 0.2613), respectively. These estimates address gene ordering within each organoid and are not directly comparable to the original macro target-wise correlations of 0.1518 and 0.1015.The archived lineage-only predictions yielded mean within-organoid correlations of 0.2745 in Broad and 0.3884 in Sanger. Expression-minus-lineage differences were +0.0684 (95% CI, 0.0334 to 0.1032) and +0.0411 (95% CI, 0.0167 to 0.0656), respectively. Thus, full-panel gene ranking showed a modest retrospective gain over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts (Table S17). This finding does not change the uncertainty in the original Sanger target-wise expression-minus-lineage difference.Top-three overlap was 34.04% in Broad and 42.79% in Sanger, compared with 34.75% and 35.36% for lineage-only prediction (Table S18). Paired expression-minus-lineage differences were −0.71 percentage points (95% CI, −4.96 to 3.19) in Broad and +7.43 percentage points (95% CI, 4.28 to 10.74) in Sanger. The Broad interval included zero; superiority for selecting the three strongest measured dependencies was therefore not demonstrated across both cohorts.Averaging the 20-gene vectors within each Sanger donor before evaluation gave a mean within-donor correlation of 0.4338 (95% CI, 0.3986 to 0.4675). The paired difference from lineage-only prediction was +0.0402 (95% CI, 0.0157 to 0.0652). Mean top-three overlap was 42.82%, with an expression-minus-lineage difference of +6.94 percentage points (95% CI, 4.17 to 9.95; Table S19). These results were consistent with the organoid-weighted analysis. All within-organoid findings remain retrospective and restricted to the selected 20-gene panel.

SECTION Sec7 Organoid core fitness genesWe applied the Adaptive Daisy Model (ADaM) to define core fitness genes in organoids, and compared these with those in cell lines9. This identified 654 shared core fitness genes and 97 that were unique to organoids (Supplementary Table 4). Gene set enrichment analysis of organoid-specific core fitness genes highlighted strong associations with steroid biosynthesis (most significant: Biological Process—steroid biosynthetic process, P value = 1.38 × 10−6; most enriched: Biological Process—isopentenyl diphosphate biosynthetic process, enrichment fold change = 667.5, Fisher’s exact test), potentially linked with a role for cholesterol in regulating intestinal stem cells and tumourgenesis46 (Extended Data Fig. 9a and Supplementary Table 4).Extended Data Fig. 9Organoid-specific core fitness genes and gene-biomarker associations.a. Essential, non-essential and genes untested in organoids owing to single guide RNA (sgRNA) selection were excluded, and compared with pan-cancer core fitness genes from cell lines. Dot size indicates the number of genes per pathway (gene names displayed), while colour represents the FDR-adjusted p-value after Fisher’s exact test. Only pathways with FDR < 10% are shown. All box plots display the median, first and third quartiles (boxes), and whiskers are 1.5x the interquartile range from the first and third quartiles.Genetic constraint, derived from population-scale human genome sequencing, reflects the degree to which a gene is intolerant to heterozygous variation and provides an orthogonal method to identify disease-linked or functionally important (essential) genes47,48. Core fitness genes experimentally derived from CRISPR–Cas9 screens in cell lines9 and organoids (this study) were enriched for genetically constrained genes (high categories), as were reference lists of essential genes (Fig. 4e). By additionally excluding genes commonly essential in cell lines (area under the curve (AUC) method), we refined our list to include 18 of 97 organoid-specific core fitness genes and annotated them with mouse knockout phenotypes and GTEx tissue-specific expression (Extended Data Fig. 9b). Genes with low constraint and normal mouse knockout phenotype, such as isopentenyl diphosphate delta isomerase 1 (IDI1), required for isoprenoid synthesis and involved in cholesterol production, may reflect cancer organoid selective fitness dependencies. Conversely, genes under high genetic constraint and with severe knockout phenotypes represent candidate core fitness genes identified in organoids—for example, ITGB1 (Extended Data Fig. 9b,c). Together, this integrative approach combining experimental data from organoids with genetic constraint from human populations identifies core fitness genes.
SECTION Sec11 DiscussionReductionist models are central to cancer biology and drug discovery. However, cancer heterogeneity strongly influences prognosis and treatment response, creating a need for larger, more representative model collections to advance precision medicine. Our comprehensive, highly annotated biobank complements 2D cell lines and is designed to catalyse discovery. To maximize access, models are deposited in public repositories and datasets are available via the Cell Model Passport40 and DepMap Miner (https://dataminer.depmap.sanger.ac.uk/) portals.This study is distinctive for the number of highly annotated organoids and the open availability of detailed genomic, patient and clinical data for each organoid10. Future biobanking would benefit from deeper tumour annotation, including histology, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and matched stromal and immune cultures54. We used tissue-specific, standardized conditions to generate a molecularly diverse biobank and enable cross-model comparisons. Tailored culture conditions may enrich specific molecular subtypes and alter gene dependencies55, and xenotransplantation provides an in vivo context to assess microenvironmental effects.Genome-wide CRISPR screens in tumour organoids are rare42,56, yet we map dependencies across a diverse biobank and achieved cell line-level quality despite the added complexity of 3D culture. Distinguishing cancer-selective dependencies from core fitness genes may inform therapeutic index, although matched normal cells are rarely available. To strengthen interpretation, we integrated population-scale genetic constraint data48, providing orthogonal support for core fitness genes and indirect evidence of target tolerability.Our organoid dependency map identified novel and clinically relevant vulnerabilities. We found allele-specific differences in KRAS and EGFR dependencies, with KRASG12X variants showing greater reliance on KRAS and upstream EGFR signalling. This supports a model53,57 in which G12X tumours remain responsive to upstream receptor activation, unlike signalling-independent Q61X variants, with therapeutic implications for targeting KRASG12X cancers, and has been proposed to underlie the enrichment of KRASQ61X mutations as secondary resistance events to EGFR inhibitors in colorectal cancer. Additionally, by generating and dependency mapping patient-matched organoids before and after treatment, we traced tumour evolution under therapeutic pressure and uncovered new hypotheses for intervention in treatment-refractory ESCA. In summary, we provide a preview of a cancer dependency map across a diverse cohort of highly annotated organoid cultures, with potential to enhance and extend existing efforts as a tool for discovery.Large-scale sequencing efforts58,59 defined tumour mutational landscapes and transformed understanding of cancer biology. A next frontier in precision oncology is to move beyond descriptive genomics towards multi-scale, integrative functional maps that enable mechanistic modelling of disease, including virtual cell frameworks60,61. This will require systematic modelling and perturbation across representative tumour cohorts integrated with patient data. Our organoid biobank and dependency map mark a major step towards building functionally informed maps of human cancer.
SECTION Sec36 Analysis of organoid core fitness genesWe applied ADaM implemented in the CoRe R package (v1.0.0) (https://github.com/DepMap-Analytics/CoRe)98 using the same curated reference essential gene set as previously mentioned3 to calculate false-positive rates. This analysis identified 751 core essential genes (Supplementary table 4). Although we used all organoids together as input, only three cancer types were included (PAAD and STAD organoids were excluded), so the resulting core fitness genes do not represent a pan-cancer set.We compared core fitness genes in organoids with those identified in cell lines9 and observed an overlap of 654 genes, with 97 genes identified as organoid-specific (Extended Data Fig. 9). We performed a Fisher’s exact test on these organoid-specific core fitness genes to perform pathway enrichment analysis, using Gene Ontology Biological Processes, KEGG pathways99 and Hallmarks100 obtained from the msigdbr R package (v7.5.1)101. For this analysis, PanCancer common essential genes identified using the AUC method were excluded98. For visualization, when multiple pathways shared the same set of organoid-specific core fitness genes, only the pathway with the most significant P value was displayed.
SECTION Sec38 Biomarker analysisTo identify molecular and clinical features associated with context-specific gene dependencies, we performed a systematic biomarker analysis across gastrointestinal, COAD/READ and ESCA organoids. Candidate dependencies were selected from the differential dependency analysis based on recurrence criteria and evaluated against a curated set of genomic, transcriptomic and clinical features, including driver mutations and specific variants, copy number alterations, structural events, mutational signatures, gene expression, pathway activity scores, and composite loss- and gain-of-function events. Associations between gene fitness effects and features were tested using linear regression models incorporating relevant technical and biological covariates, with significance assessed using likelihood-ratio tests and multiple testing correction. Significant associations were prioritized based on adjusted P value and effect size and classified into tiers reflecting strength of association. Full details of feature selection, model specification, statistical thresholds and classification criteria are provided in the Supplementary Information.
